details:
WHAT IT DOES

LUNA NAV is an interactive lunar landing-site navigator. For any location on the Moon and any date, it answers two questions: how much sunlight will the site receive, and when is Earth visible for direct-to-Earth communication? Users explore a 3D lunar globe, a 2D south-polar map with NASA Moon Trek imagery, and a local-horizon skyplot showing the Sun and Earth. They can compare two scenarios (same site on different dates, or different sites), enter custom coordinates, estimate solar power for a vertical mast versus a flat panel under grazing polar light, find windows when sunlight and an Earth link coincide, and export a mission report. The app includes 11 curated sites: Artemis candidates, historic landings, a commercial CLPS landing and a farside mission.

HOW IT WORKS

A Node/Express backend queries the NASA JPL Horizons API (DE441 ephemeris) for sub-solar and sub-Earth points and true Sun-Moon and Earth-Moon distances. Requests are cached and throttled to respect NASA's service. From these, the app computes the Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth at the chosen site. If Horizons is unreachable, an offline solver based on IAU rotational elements and Meeus algorithms takes over. We validated this solver against Horizons over 10 epochs of one lunar cycle (mean sub-solar latitude error about 0.014 degrees, longitude about 0.83 degrees; details in docs/VALIDATION.md).

DATA HONESTY

Every value is labeled by source: LIVE (JPL Horizons), COMPUTED (IAU/Meeus models), CURATED (published mission literature) or IMAGERY (NASA Moon Trek, NASA SVS). Limitations are stated in the app: calculations use a mean spherical Moon, so local terrain shadowing and horizon masks are not included, and site elevations are nominal literature values, not sampled from LOLA.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

LUNA NAV makes polar illumination and Earth-visibility concepts accessible to students, educators and early-stage mission planners, with Beginner and Technical modes. It helps users see why the lunar south pole is attractive (near-continuous sunlight on ridges, nearby cold traps) and why it is difficult (grazing light, intermittent Earth visibility).

TOOLS

React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, Leaflet, Recharts, Node.js, Express, NASA JPL Horizons API, NASA Moon Trek WMTS, NASA SVS lunar basemap, Jean Meeus's Astronomical Algorithms, IAU/IAG rotational elements. Source code: https://github.com/Bhaumikwahi7/luna-nav

CREATIVITY

We combined a live ephemeris, a physical power model and a provenance system in one tool. The vertical-mast versus flat-panel comparison shows quickly why polar landers use tall solar arrays, and the provenance badges let users see which numbers are measured, computed or taken from literature.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty over polish, graceful offline fallback, respecting NASA API limits, simple language for beginners alongside exact angles for experts, and clear caveats about what the model does not yet include.

FUTURE WORK

Sampling LOLA digital elevation models, 360-degree horizon raytracing for true terrain line-of-sight, and validation across 2026 to 2035.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

Code, documentation and parts of the text were developed with AI assistance (Claude and an AI coding agent). All outputs were reviewed and tested by the team.
